texto: It is a warm summer night. You flip on the porch light,
and within minutes, they arrive.
Moths. Dozens of them. Spinning around the bulb,
bumping into the glass, never landing, never leaving.
In the morning, a few are still there, stuck flat against the wall.
So what happens to a moth that circles
your porch light all night long? And why can't it just fly away?
For centuries, people said moths love the light.
In twenty twenty-four, scientists finally filmed it in three dimensions.
And it turns out, they don't.
They are not attracted. They are trapped.
The old idea was that moths steer by the moon.
Keep the moon at the same angle, and you fly in a straight line.
Mistake a bulb for the moon, and you spiral into it.
It sounded smart. But when researchers from
Imperial College London tracked insects around lights with
motion capture cameras, that is not what they saw.
Here is what really happens.
For millions of years, the brightest thing in the night was the sky.
So the brightest direction meant up. To stay level,
flying insects tilt their backs toward the brightest light.
It is like an autopilot that keeps them right side up.
Now put a bright bulb next to a moth. Its autopilot
says the sky is over there, sideways. So it tilts its back toward the bulb.
And it ends up flying in circles around it.
Orbiting. Stuck. When it passes right over the top,
it can even flip upside down, because now the
sky seems to be below it. The researchers saw the same
thing in moths, dragonflies and other night fliers.
Imagine driving home at night with your GPS
stuck on turn left. Forever.
So the moth circles. And circles. Burning energy it
needed for finding food and finding a mate.
Some fall out of the air, exhausted.
Others finally land on the wall, and freeze until morning.
And at dawn, a pale moth on a bright wall has nowhere to hide.
Birds and lizards know exactly where to look.
Even at night, a light full of moths is a buffet.
Bats swoop in. And spiders build their webs
right next to the bulb. And every moth stuck at
your porch is a moth that is not out there doing its job.
And this matters more than it seems.
Moths are the night shift of pollination. While bees sleep,
moths carry pollen from flower to flower.
In England, another team found that moths visit a huge variety
of wild flowers, carrying pollen across whole fields in the dark.
In one experiment in Switzerland, meadows
lit up at night got sixty-two percent fewer
visits from night pollinators.
And one of the plants there made thirteen percent less fruit.
Just because of the lights.
So what can you do? It is surprisingly easy.
Turn the porch light off when nobody needs it, or put it on a motion sensor.
Swap the bright white bulb for a warm yellow one.
Fewer insects get caught in its spell.
And point your lights down, toward the ground, not up into the sky.
That keeps the fake sky out of their eyes.
Even closing the curtains helps, so the lights inside your house do
not spill out into the yard.
So the next time you see a moth spinning around your porch light,
you will know the truth. It is not in love with the light.
It is lost, flying in circles,
trying to keep the sky on top. Flip the switch, and let it find
the real one.
